summary: Defines some common media features for describing image resolution, size, color and image representation methods that are common to web browsing, printing and fax applications.

plainLanguage.summary: These tags let a device describe itself before it is sent something. A phone says how many pixels its screen has, a printer says its resolution and paper size, and the sender then picks a version that suits the recipient.

subtitle: Named tags that let a device say what it can display or print, so the sender can pick the right version.

tldr.problem: A sender cannot choose a suitable version of a document unless it knows what the recipient can handle, and the requirements of web browsers to report display characteristics were the original motivation for media features.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers six feature tags inside the registration framework of RFC 2506: pix-x, pix-y, dpi, ua-media, paper-size and color. Each tag has an ASN.1 identifier and a defined set of value types, such as a signed integer, a rational, or a token with an equality relationship.
tldr.outcome: A recipient can describe its screen size, resolution, device medium, paper size and colour capability, and a sender can then choose between higher and lower resolution renditions. The RFC notes that inaccurate feature information can cause a denial of service.

sections.title: What a Media Feature Is
sections.content:
This work was originally motivated by the requirements from web browsers to send the browser's display characteristics to the web server, so the server could choose an appropriate representation. A media feature is a tag by which a recipient informs a sender of the characteristics of its message handling. The sender may then provide the variant of the message that is most suitable for the recipient.

Different variants would typically be higher or lower resolution images. In the case of sending to a printer the result would be higher quality output; in the case of a small screen device such as a cellphone or portable digital assistant the result would be faster transmission.

Media features may be used in many different protocol situations. Each registration in Section 2 follows the form specified in RFC 2506 and gives the feature tag name, the ASN.1 identifier associated with the tag, a summary of what the tag indicates, the values appropriate for it, the applications it is intended for, and examples of typical use. The document calls for registration of the six feature tags pix-x, pix-y, dpi, ua-media, paper-size and color, with an ASN.1 identifier assigned to each and replaced in the body of the registration.
sections.plainLanguage: A feature tag is a label with a fixed meaning, so that any two programs agree what it says. A sender reads the labels the receiver sent and chooses the matching version of the document.

sections.title: Image Size: pix-x and pix-y
sections.content:
The tags pix-x and pix-y have ASN.1 identifiers 1.3.6.1.8.1.1 and 1.3.6.1.8.1.2. They indicate the display size of the recipient for display or print, measured in pixels, with pix-x giving the horizontal dimension and pix-y the vertical one. The value appropriate for these tags is a signed integer.

They are intended for display and print applications where different media choices are made depending on the size of the recipient device. A web application for use on a 240x480 display might use different HTML pages than one intended for use on a 1024x768 display.
sections.plainLanguage: Two numbers say how wide and how tall the screen is, counted in pixels. The sender uses them to pick a page that fits.

sections.title: Resolution: dpi
sections.content:
The tag dpi has ASN.1 identifier 1.3.6.1.8.1.3. It indicates the resolution that the recipient can display or print without loss, measured in pixels per inch. Resolution capability is typically represented as dots per inch rather than in SI units, and values for dpi may be expressed as a rational to accommodate resolution of SI-based devices: the RFC gives dpi=19558/100 as the way to represent a resolution of 77 dots per centimeter. The value appropriate for the tag is a rational.

Printing and fax applications typically choose representations of a transmitted document depending on the resolution of the recipient rather than pixel size, for example choosing a version of a printable document to send to a printer. Software applications are typically unaware of the resolution of the display. Devices exist with different resolution in different directions, so that individual pixels are not square, but this feature only encompasses the uniform resolution.
sections.plainLanguage: Resolution says how many dots fit into an inch. It matters most for printers and faxes, which choose a sharper or a softer version of a document depending on what the machine can handle.

sections.title: Device Medium: ua-media
sections.content:
The tag ua-media has ASN.1 identifier 1.3.6.1.8.1.4. It indicates the recipient's device medium with a simple token. The values are a token with an equality relationship:

  • screen, a refreshable display;
  • screen-paged, a refreshable display which cannot scroll;
  • stationery, separately cut sheets of an opaque material;
  • transparency, separately cut sheets of a transparent material;
  • envelope, envelopes that can be used for conventional mailing purposes;
  • envelope-plain, envelopes that are not preprinted and have no windows;
  • continuous, continuously connected sheets of an opaque material.

Most of the values are useful for printing applications, or to distinguish printing from display. A typical use is selecting between a rendition intended to be printed and one intended to be displayed. Other media values were not included because their utility seemed relative. Interoperability with the Internet Print Protocol means that some additional feature values may need to be registered.
sections.plainLanguage: This tag says what the output is: a screen, a sheet of paper, a transparency, an envelope. It is what lets the sender choose a printable version instead of a screen version.

sections.title: Paper Size: paper-size
sections.content:
The tag paper-size has ASN.1 identifier 1.3.6.1.8.1.5. For stationery it is often useful to have information about the size of the output. While it is more precise and predictable to use absolute resolution and pixel sizes, some applications find it useful to provide paper size in addition to this information. Not all of the paper may have a printable area.

The values are a token with an equality relationship. Typical values are letter at 8.5x11.0 inches, a4 at 210x297 mm, b4 at 250x353 mm, a3 at 297x420 mm, and legal at 8.5x14 inches. The tag seems most useful for the printing application, for example choosing between a4 and letter size renditions of the same printable document.
sections.plainLanguage: One more token names the paper: letter, a4, legal and so on, each with its measurements. A sender can then offer the version that matches the paper in the tray.

sections.title: Colour and Greyscale: color
sections.content:
The tag color has ASN.1 identifier 1.3.6.1.8.1.6. It indicates a gross level of capability to represent, or need for, handling of colour, out of a limited set of choices. The values are a token with an equality relationship:

  • binary, black-and-white or other bi-level capability;
  • grey, more than two levels of intensity, for example at least two bits of grey-scale data;
  • limited, availability of a small number of colours, such as a highlight printer, pen plotter or limited colour display. At the lowest level this implies at least one colour other than black, and at the high end a small number, less than 32, of colours. No implication is made that any particular colour is available;
  • mapped, pixel colour values are mapped in some specifiable way to a multi-component colour space. Sufficient levels of display are available to represent a continuous tone photographic image, but the result will be mapped into a more limited space;
  • full, the ability, or at least the willingness, to represent a full colour image and present it, with full continuous tone colour capability.

Web applications may choose between colour, grey or binary representations, and fax or printing applications might choose between colour and non-colour renditions. The intended usage of the tag is COMMON.
sections.plainLanguage: Five levels of colour, from plain black and white up to a full colour photograph. The tag says how much colour the recipient can take, so the sender does not send a picture it cannot use.

sections.title: Examples of Feature Comparison
sections.content:
The RFC gives three example comparisons that show how the features describe capabilities. The syntax used to express combinations of features is purely illustrative and not normative.

pix-x<=1024, pix-y<=768
   might be used for a 1024x768 display.

dpi=300
   might be used for a 300 dpi printer.

paper-size=a4
   indicates the display size is 210x297mm.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples read as plain conditions: a screen no wider than 1024 pixels, a printer that does 300 dots per inch, or a sheet of A4 paper.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Inaccurate media feature information ascribed to a recipient might cause a sender to subsequently send content that the recipient is not actually able to process, thus causing a denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: If the description of the recipient is wrong, the sender may send something the recipient cannot handle. That is the one security risk the RFC points out.
